content: The recruitment process will be explained to participants, and they will be provided with coupons as part of the study. An optimal survey site should have multiple interview rooms and designated spaces for pre-test and post-test counseling, specimen collection, and conducting any necessary tests. A bathroom must be available for participants' convenience and for the collection of urine specimens. A kitchen is beneficial for preparing refreshments for participants waiting in the reception area and can also serve as a break room for survey staff. Depending on the biomarkers included in the survey, a small laboratory space may also be required. For more detailed information on survey sites and staffing positions required for an RDS (Respondent-Driven Sampling) survey, refer to the section on staff selection in Chapter A-14. The layout of an RDS site should include specific areas such as interview rooms, a kitchen, a bathroom, counseling rooms, a specimen collection room, an entrance, a reception/waiting area, and a space for a coupon manager. Seed selection is a critical component of the RDS recruitment process. Seeds are members of the target population who are invited by survey investigators to initiate the recruitment process. Factors to consider when selecting seeds include the number of seeds, their diversity in characteristics, and their likelihood of recruiting others. Selecting too many seeds may overwhelm the survey site with participants, potentially reaching the target sample size before achieving equilibrium. Conversely, selecting too few seeds may delay reaching the desired sample size and result in underrepresentation of certain social networks. The number of seeds required depends on factors such as the calculated sample size, the level of compensation offered, and the number of connections within the survey population. A larger sample size may necessitate more seeds, while higher compensation can motivate participation but may also attract ineligible individuals. If the population has extensive social networks, fewer seeds may be needed to sustain recruitment. Diversity among seeds is not mandatory but is advantageous for faster convergence toward equilibrium. Seeds should represent a variety of socially significant variables, such as HIV status, socioeconomic status, age, gender, and sexual identity. For example, in studies involving men who have sex with men (MSM), it is important to include both gay-identified and non-gay-identified men as seeds. Ideal seeds are well-connected within their social networks, trusted, well-liked, and effective communicators who can promote survey participation. They should be well-informed about the survey and enthusiastic about recruiting others. Organizations or groups closely associated with the target population can assist in identifying suitable seeds. Seeds should have large social networks and be capable of recruiting participants effectively. The sample should ideally represent a complete network component. Compensation for participation in an RDS survey is strongly recommended, though not mandatory. The amount and type of compensation should be determined based on findings from formative assessments and included in the survey protocol. Compensation should be sufficient to acknowledge participants' time and effort without incentivizing participation solely for monetary gain or encouraging fraudulent behavior, such as duplicate participation or the buying and selling of coupons. Compensation should reflect respect for participants' contributions and their judgment in using the remuneration for personal needs. Personal network size, defined as the number of people a participant knows who are likely eligible for the survey, is a crucial metric for weighting the data. Questions about personal network size should be asked face-to-face, even in surveys using audio computer-assisted self-interviewing (ACASI), to allow participants to seek clarification if needed. Examples of network size questions include: How many people do you know who have sold sex in the past six months? and Of these, how many live in this city? These questions help determine the weights used for data analysis. Eligible participants should be assigned a unique participant code (UPC) to verify their identity during subsequent visits. The UPC can be created using answers to personal questions known only to the participant, such as the first two letters of their first name, the first two letters of their mother’s name, their age at the time of the initial interview, and the first two letters of their mother’s place of birth. Alternatively, some surveys use fingerprint scanners to generate a unique alphanumeric code without storing the actual fingerprint image, ensuring anonymity. This code can be regenerated during a second visit to retrieve the participant’s record. Guidelines for reporting RDS data and analyzing it are available, including resources from the World Health Organization (WHO) and the University of California, San Francisco. These resources provide comprehensive guidance on RDS methodology, data analysis, and reporting. Sample size requirements for probability-based surveys, including one-time and repeated surveys, should be informed by statistical and resource considerations. While software packages and online calculators are available for sample size calculations, consulting a statistician is advisable, especially for complex survey designs. Key terms such as confidence interval, design effect, and precision are essential for understanding and interpreting survey results.
